mcqs.question: Why is the average jobs/sec figure (e.g. 116 jobs/sec) insufficient for sizing a distributed job scheduler?
options: The average figure is always an overestimate of true load
Real workloads cluster around common schedule times (like midnight), producing short bursts far above the daily average that the system must also absorb
Job scheduling systems never experience variable load in practice
The average only matters for billing purposes, not system capacity
mcqs.explanation: Scheduled workloads bunch up around common times ('run at midnight'), so peak load during those bursts can be many times the smoothed daily average — sizing only for the average leaves the system unable to absorb the burst. The average isn't an overestimate, load absolutely varies over the day, and this is a capacity concern, not a billing one.

mcqs.question: Why must exactly one scheduler instance hold leadership when deciding which jobs are due, rather than letting multiple instances poll independently?
options: Multiple instances polling independently would each dispatch the same due jobs, causing accidental duplicate execution before any worker-level lease is even involved
Only one scheduler instance is ever allowed to run at a time, by cloud provider policy
Polling the job table is too slow for more than one instance to do concurrently
Leader election is only needed to reduce network bandwidth usage
mcqs.explanation: Without a single leader, two scheduler instances could both see the same job as due and both dispatch it, creating duplicate execution at the scheduling layer itself — a distinct problem from worker-level lease collisions. There's no cloud-provider single-instance rule, polling speed isn't the bottleneck here, and bandwidth isn't the driver.

mcqs.question: Thousands of jobs are all scheduled for exactly midnight, causing the job store to buckle under a burst of simultaneous dispatch requests. What is the standard fix?
options: Reject all jobs scheduled for the same exact time
Add small random jitter to each job's actual dispatch time within its due window, spreading the instantaneous spike into a smoother burst
Permanently increase the job store's capacity to handle worst-case midnight load year-round
Force all jobs to run sequentially, one at a time, regardless of schedule
mcqs.explanation: Jitter is the standard fix: spreading exact-same-time jobs across a small window turns a stampede into a manageable burst, at the cost of small scheduling imprecision most jobs don't care about. Rejecting same-time jobs breaks legitimate use cases, over-provisioning for a rare peak wastes resources most of the time, and forcing full seriality throws away the fleet's parallelism entirely.
